author: Thousifa Mohammad, open to work
text:
🚀 The Future of AI Isn't Just Bigger Models—It's Smarter AI Systems.
Over the past year, the conversation has shifted from simply using Large Language Models (LLMs) to building production-ready AI systems that can reason, retrieve, automate, and continuously improve.
Some of the most exciting trends shaping AI today:
✅ AI Agents capable of planning and executing multi-step workflows
✅ Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for trustworthy enterprise AI
✅ Multimodal AI that understands text, images, audio, and documents together
✅ LLMOps for monitoring, evaluation, guardrails, and responsible AI deployment
✅ Open-source models becoming increasingly competitive alongside frontier models
Building AI today isn't just about prompting an LLM—it's about designing reliable systems that combine machine learning, data engineering, cloud infrastructure, and user experience into solutions that create measurable business impact.
As an AI/ML & GenAI Engineer, I'm passionate about developing scalable AI applications using technologies such as Python, FastAPI, LangChain, GPT-4, AWS, Azure, vector databases, and MLOps to solve real-world challenges.
The AI landscape is evolving faster than ever, and continuous learning remains the greatest competitive advantage.
💬 What AI trend do you believe will have the biggest impact over the next two years—AI Agents, multimodal AI, open-source LLMs, or autonomous software engineering?
Let's connect and exchange ideas!

author: Bala Sai Chaitanya Tupakula
text:
📈 5 Cloud & DevOps Trends Every Senior Engineer Should Watch in 2026 🚀
Cloud and DevOps are evolving rapidly, and enterprise hiring is increasingly focused on engineers who can combine automation, scalability, and AI-driven operations.

🔥 1. Platform Engineering is on the rise
Companies are building Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) to improve developer productivity and accelerate delivery.

☸️ 2. Kubernetes skills remain essential
Cloud-native applications and container orchestration continue to dominate modern infrastructure.

🏗️ 3. Infrastructure as Code is a must-have
Terraform and automated infrastructure provisioning are now standard across enterprise environments.

☁️ 4. Multi-Cloud expertise adds significant value
Experience with AWS, Azure, and GCP is highly sought after for large-scale transformation initiatives.

🤖 5. AI Infrastructure & MLOps are reshaping Cloud Engineering
AI workloads, GPU infrastructure, ML pipelines, and cloud-native AI services are creating exciting opportunities for senior engineers.

💡 The Bottom Line:
The most in-demand Cloud & DevOps professionals are those who understand cloud architecture, automation, security, observability, and AI-powered infrastructure.

💬 Which of these trends is impacting your projects the most? Share your thoughts in the comments!

author: Lakhan Jadhav
text:
🚀 OPEN TO WORK | Senior AI/ML Engineer | Generative AI | Agentic AI | MLOps

I'm actively exploring opportunities as a Senior AI/ML Engineer, Generative AI Engineer, or Staff Machine Learning Engineer.

With 9+ years of experience, I've architected and deployed enterprise AI solutions across Banking, Healthcare, Insurance, and Capital Markets. My expertise spans Generative AI, LLMs, Agentic AI, GraphRAG, LangChain, LangGraph, Python, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Kubernetes, AWS, Azure, GCP, and enterprise MLOps.

One production challenge that reshaped how I think about enterprise AI platforms was this:

Improving one AI capability had the potential to impact dozens of business applications.

A newer model was available.
Evaluation metrics were better.
Internal testing showed promising results.
But the platform wasn't serving just one application.
Multiple products, internal teams, and business workflows depended on the same AI services.

A direct upgrade could introduce unexpected behavioral changes across the organization.

I worked on implementing model versioning, application-specific compatibility testing, phased deployments, release monitoring, and rollback strategies so each consuming application could transition at its own pace without disrupting business operations.

The objective wasn't simply:
"Can we deploy the latest model?"

The better question was:
"Can we evolve the AI platform while protecting every application that depends on it?"

That experience reinforced an important lesson:
Enterprise AI isn't built around individual models. It's built around stable platforms that enable many teams to innovate with confidence.

As AI adoption grows across an organization, platform engineering, governance, and operational discipline become just as valuable as advances in model performance.

These are the engineering challenges I enjoy solving, and I'm excited to bring this experience to my next opportunity.

If your organization is hiring for AI, Machine Learning, Generative AI, Agentic AI, or MLOps roles, I'd welcome the opportunity to connect.

author: Divyanshe Agrawal
text:
🚀 IT Hiring Trends in 2026 – What Every Tech Professional, Recruiter & Employer Should Know

💻 As an IT Recruiter, one question keeps coming up in almost every conversation:
👉 "Is IT hiring slowing down in 2026?"
👉 "Which skills are actually in demand?"
👉 "Will AI replace software engineers?"
👉 "Should I upskill or wait for the market to improve?"

The truth is...
IT hiring isn't disappearing—it's transforming.

Companies are hiring more strategically, with a stronger focus on niche skills and business impact than ever before.

Here are the biggest IT hiring trends shaping 2026.

🤖 1️⃣ AI Skills Are No Longer Optional
Generative AI, LLMs, AI Agents, Prompt Engineering, and AI-powered automation have become key hiring priorities. Recent hiring data shows AI-related recruitment continues to grow even while overall IT hiring remains selective.

☁️ 2️⃣ Cloud & Cybersecurity Continue to Dominate
Organizations are investing heavily in cloud modernization, cybersecurity, and digital transformation, creating sustained demand for professionals with AWS, Azure, GCP, DevSecOps, and security expertise.

📊 3️⃣ Data Is the New Competitive Advantage
Data Engineers, Data Scientists, Analytics Engineers, and ML Engineers remain among the most sought-after professionals as companies increasingly rely on data-driven decision-making.

💡 Think of it this way:
👨‍💻 Developers build solutions.
🏢 Companies build innovative products.

🤝 IT Recruiters connect the right talent with the right opportunities.
Together, they drive the future of technology.

One thing is absolutely clear:

In 2026, companies aren't just hiring coders—they're hiring problem solvers, AI-ready professionals, and lifelong learners.

As an IT Recruiter, I've noticed that candidates who combine strong technical fundamentals with AI knowledge, communication skills, and business understanding are standing out in today's competitive market.

🙏 Technology will continue to evolve, but one thing won't change—the willingness to learn will always be the most valuable skill.

🤝 Thodi knowledge aapki, thodi knowledge meri… aur milkar banayenge ek aur bhi knowledgeable LinkedIn family! 💙

author: Betsy Tong
text:
MIT just dropped 10 free AI courses.
Most leaders will ignore them.
They’re not lazy.

They just assume this is for engineers.
It’s not.

If you approve budgets, set direction, or manage people, AI literacy is not optional.

You don’t need to code.
But you do need to know when someone is hiding behind language.

“AI-powered.”
“Foundation model.”
“Proprietary algorithm.”

Those words are meant to activate your belief in meetings.
They also hide risk.

The fastest way to spot overselling isn’t hiring another consultant.
It’s spending 60 minutes with the fundamentals.

When you understand one layer deeper:
You stop asking:
❌ “Is this cutting-edge?”

You start asking:
✅ “What data is it trained on?”
✅ “What does it fail at?”
✅ “What does it cost to run at scale?”
✅ “What decisions does this actually automate?”

That shift changes how IT and vendors talk to you.

Intro-level AI literacy isn’t ambition.
It’s control.

Here are 10 MIT courses worth scanning.
Not to become technical.
To stop being boxed in by technical language:

1️⃣ AI 101 – Never get snowed by vendors again
👉 https://lnkd.in/gyJz7whc

2️⃣ Artificial Intelligence – Separate real from hype
👉 https://lnkd.in/ggneRvcZ

3️⃣ Foundation Models & Generative AI – Spot overselling instantly
👉 https://lnkd.in/gNwgbtaE

4️⃣ Introduction to Machine Learning – Fund the right bets
👉 https://lnkd.in/gT5HcRs5

5️⃣ Understanding the World Through Data – Ask sharper questions
👉 https://lnkd.in/gVdj_EhG

6️⃣ Introduction to Deep Learning – Know what actually costs millions
👉 https://lnkd.in/gq8PwrnP

7️⃣ ML with Python – See if your team is building or spinning
👉 https://lnkd.in/gUdHfAhx

8️⃣ How to AI (Almost) Anything – Find competitive whitespace
👉 https://lnkd.in/ghfgKgsx

9️⃣ Introduction to Algorithms – Defend AI decisions under scrutiny
👉 https://lnkd.in/g2P-3ptd

🔟 AI in K-12 Education – Watch transformation before it hits you
👉 https://lnkd.in/gs9Fesqy

In 2026, “non-technical” won’t protect anyone who signs off on AI spend.

You don’t need depth.
You need enough understanding that no one can snow you.

author: Garett Moreau 🇺🇸
text:
SKILLS DRIFT: I've got a slightly contrary take on the cysec skills gap issue. We know it requires more budget and time to train up. But #cybersecurity isn’t suffering because people lack expertise. It’s more because the definition of expertise keeps mutating faster than orgs can update their job architecture. 

AI governance roles didn’t exist four years ago. AI/ML security specialists weren’t standard hires. Regulatory frameworks like NIS2, DORA, and DoD 8140 are rewriting what “qualified” even means. The workforce isn’t short on talent as much as it’s short on alignment. In other words, teams are structured around legacy assumptions.

The real bottleneck I see is that companies are still hiring for yesterday’s threat model while operating inside today’s regulatory model and defending against tomorrow’s AI‑accelerated threat model. That "temporal mismatch" creates a workforce problem no amount of budget can solve.

Titles that once made sense (analyst, engineer, architect) now hide wildly different responsibilities depending on the organization. AI governance, ML security, exposure management, cloud‑native detection, etc. 

These are not “specializations.” They’re entirely new disciplines. Yet most companies still write job descriptions as if the environment were frozen in 2019. But you may disagree, let me know.

author: Amit Goel, open to work
text:
Is the growth of Global Capability Centers (GCCs) slowing down in Bengaluru? 

Let's start with the facts: Bengaluru remains a leader with over 875 GCCs, accounting for approximately 27-36% of the national base, and nearly 50% of India's AI/ML talent. The city hosts 27% of all Indian GCCs and 37% of GCC talent. However, Hyderabad and Pune are experiencing faster growth from a smaller base, attracting new openings for various reasons. 

In the first two months of 2026 alone, three major GCCs launched in Hyderabad, solidifying its position as India's fastest-growing GCC destination. While Bengaluru excels in expansions and AI-specific mandates, Hyderabad is capturing a significant share of new logos. 

Why are companies choosing Hyderabad and Pune over Bengaluru? 
- **Cost**: Pune offers 20-30% lower costs than Bengaluru, with attrition around 14%. A 100-engineer center in Pune is significantly cheaper annually than in Bengaluru. 
- **Attrition**: Bengaluru's attrition often exceeds 20% for competitive engineering roles, with aggressive counter-offers. In contrast, Bengaluru and Hyderabad's attrition ranges from 16-18%, prompting GCCs to establish satellite locations. 
- **Infrastructure/Talent Saturation**: Metro hubs are becoming saturated, leading to tighter competition in real estate, commuting, and hiring pools in Bengaluru. 
- **Policy Push**: Hyderabad benefits from a policy-driven, digital-first ecosystem with strong BFSI presence, supported by initiatives like the Telangana AI Mission and AI City, providing a balanced cost-to-capability advantage. 
- **Domain Fit**: Pune has evolved into a hub for enterprise services and shared operations, while Hyderabad excels in life sciences and biotech due to its Genome Valley ecosystem. 

The trend is shifting towards a hub-and-spoke model, where leadership remains in Bengaluru or Hyderabad, engineering scales in Pune or Chennai, and cost-efficient back-office work is moved to tier-2 cities. This indicates that Bengaluru is not losing its significance but rather narrowing its role to leadership and AI-core functions. 

Looking ahead, Bengaluru will likely maintain its #1 position but may see its share soften. It will continue to dominate in AI/ML, deep-tech, and Fortune 500 engineering HQs. The market is not moving away from Bengaluru; instead, it is transitioning to a model where Bengaluru anchors leadership and AI-core, while execution scales disperse to Pune, Hyderabad, Chennai, and tier-2 cities. 

To win GCC leadership by 2030, companies must architect their strategies across cities, maintaining leadership in Bengaluru, scaling in Pune or Hyderabad, and ensuring cost efficiency in tier-2 locations.

author: Brett Schlobohm
text:
Uber burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in four months. When its COO was asked whether all that spending was producing more value for customers, he said flatly: "That link is not there yet." One fintech employee ran up $81,267 in AI credits in a single week, building a side project. Gartner says there's "no direct relation" between token spend and productivity, and forecasts AI coding costs will pass the average developer's salary by 2028.

Here's the uncomfortable part: the problem was never the size of the bill. It's that most companies can't tell you what their AI bill actually bought. That's not a budget failure, it's an instrumentation failure, and it's the exact mirror image of the layoff mistake from Part One. My new piece breaks down the named cases, three cost scenarios a CFO can rebuild, and the fix: stop measuring cost per token and start measuring risk-adjusted cost per acceptable outcome.
